full_judgment:
9. Mr Abdul Malek, Senior Advocate with Mr KZ Alam, Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant, supports the appeal and strenuously submits that at the time of occurrence due to unsoundness of mind he was incapable of understanding the nature of the act or what he was doing was unlawful or wrong. The appellant was under the spell of mental unbalance and not capable of understanding. He added that as many as 13 prosecution witnesses were examined apart from the  police and the doctor, all other witnesses are close relations and they, in one voice, stated that the appellant used to remain almost all the time unbalanced mentally and of unsound mind. Referring to the evidence of prosecution witnesses, he submits that PW 1 Lt Col Younus Khan who is the informant of the case himself testified that in 1973-1974 the appellant became mentally unbalanced and with his help he was admitted in Combined Military Hospital (CMH) 2/3 times and even on the date of occurrence he was under the treatment of Psychiatrist in CMH and he was suffering from manic depressive psychosis. So, according to him, the appellant had been suffering from insanity at the time of occurrence and the offence allegedly committed by him will come within the general exceptions laid down in section 84 of Chapter IV of the Penal Code. He added that there is no evidence that there was any ill feeling between the relations, rather all the defence witnesses, who are responsible doctors of CMH, supported the defence version regarding unsoundness/insanity of the appellant. In support of his contentions he referred the case of Nikhil Chandra Halder vs State reported in 54 DLR 148. He added that the prosecution must prove the guilt of the accused beyond all reasonable doubt and the burden of proof never shifts and the duty is generally cast upon the prosecution to negative any special defence raised by the accused. He added that general exception and special defence plea taken by the accused does not relieve the prosecution from proving its case beyond reasonable doubt. The defence failing to prove special pleading but succeeded in raising reasonable doubt are entitled to be acquitted. In support of his contention he further referred the case of Woolmington vs Director of Public Prosecution reported in House of Lords in All England Law Reports (Reprint) page 1, Ghulam Yusaf vs Crown reported in PLD 1953 Lahore 213 and Safdar Ali vs Crown reported in 5 DLR (FC) 64. 

 40. It is well settled since Mc Naughten's case (1843) that all persons are presumed to be sane and it is for the defence to prove the insanity of the accused at the precise moment when he committed the offence although the initial burden to establish the offence is always on the prosecution who has to prove its allegations against an accused beyond reasonable doubt and such onus on the prosecution never shifts. But in contradiction to such onus on the prosecution, the burden to prove the insanity, on the part of the defence is not that onerous, the accused is required to prove his plea of insanity on the balance of probabilities on preponderance of evidence. With this regard reliance can be placed in the case of Sodeman vs R (PC) (1936) 2 All ER 1138 wherein it is held: 

 "It is certainly plain that the burden in cases in which an accused has to prove insanity may fairly be stated as not being higher than the burden which rests upon a plaintiff or defendant in civil proceedings."
